cards.heading: Definition
cards.question: What is the MCP attack surface taxonomy?
cards.answer: OWASP's MCP Top 10 — a ten-category enumeration of security risks specific to deploying MCP servers and the agents that call them, meant to be used as a design checklist and audit frame, not a one-time ranking.

cards.heading: What unifies the ten categories
cards.question: What three things does MCP concentrate at a single boundary that used to be separate, unifying all ten risk categories?
cards.answer: Credentials for downstream systems, an instruction channel the model will obey, and an execution path into shells and APIs — each category is a way one of those three escapes.

cards.heading: Tool poisoning sub-techniques
cards.question: What are the three named sub-techniques of tool poisoning in this taxonomy?
cards.answer: Rug pulls (a malicious update to an already-trusted tool), schema poisoning (corrupting an interface definition to mislead the model), and tool shadowing (a fake or duplicate tool intercepting interactions).

cards.heading: Why typed JSON doesn't stop injection
cards.question: Why is command injection still a risk even though tool arguments arrive as typed JSON?
cards.answer: The schema describes structure but says nothing about whether a value is safe to hand to a shell, so developers trust arguments whose safety was never actually validated.

cards.heading: Shadow MCP servers
cards.question: What is a "shadow MCP server" in this taxonomy?
cards.answer: An MCP server spun up outside governance with default credentials and permissive configuration — the MCP-specific form of shadow IT, treated as a first-class risk category rather than a governance footnote.

cards.heading: Citation caveat
cards.question: What caveat applies to citing this taxonomy by its numeric MCPxx identifiers?
cards.answer: It is an OWASP community project at v0.1 beta with drafting seams still visible; the categories are durable but the numbering and titles are not yet stable, so cite category names instead.
